thread.title: Conversations with AI: The Space Between Where Human Intelligence and AI Interact
thread.title_full: Conversations with AI: The Space Between Where Human Intelligence and AI Interact

author: Paul Bishop
title: Conversations with AI: The Space Between Where Human Intelligence and AI Interact
text:
This is the third in a series of Conversations with AI. Like it or not, AI is here to stay, so in this weekly column Paul Bishop, who uses AI frequently, walks us through what surprises him, teaches him, and challenges him in this new artificial intelligence journey. He tells us how ÅI can enhance our efforts rather than annihilate them. See earlier articles in this series here and here.
When I sit down with Google, I expect information. When I sit down with a calculator, I expect mathematical answers. When I sit down with AI, I increasingly expect to be… surprised .
This was not what I expected when I began seriously exploring artificial intelligence. I’d heard all the promises about speed and productivity, about doing in minutes what once took hours. Those advantages are real, and I have certainly benefited from them. What I didn’t anticipate was how often an encounter with AI would leave me with an idea I didn’t have before.
Getting an answer and discovering an idea are not the same thing. If I search Google for the population of London, I expect it to retrieve the information. If I ask a calculator to divide 473 by 17, I’m not interested in discussing the possibilities. When I open a conversation with AI, I may know what I want to talk about without knowing where the conversation will end.
Getting an answer and discovering an idea are not the same thing.
There is uncertainty in the exchange, but also promise. Making the most of the promise involved learning how I wanted AI to work with me, not simply what I wanted it to do. I didn’t want constant encouragement or to be told every idea was wonderful—both common AI defaults. If an idea didn’t work, I wanted pushback. If a paragraph was already doing its job, I didn’t want suggestions to rewrite it simply because another version was possible.
Over time, getting AI to work the way I needed instead of following its defaults led to a set of hard rules I established through prompts. Don’t change something for the sake of changing it. Don’t suggest shortening my prose simply because shorter is more efficient. When we’re exploring, help me explore rather than rushing toward a polished final product. Most importantly, don’t agree with me when your assessment is different from mine. I don’t need a cheerleader. I need something willing to push against my thinking.
I don’t need a cheerleader. I need something willing to push against my thinking.
There was one problem. Every new conversation meant starting over. Rather than explaining the same principles over and over, we established agreed-upon standards in an evolving foundation document. The document could be quickly uploaded into a new chat and we were back up to speed. This wasn’t an attempt to make AI behave perfectly. It was a way to preserve what was already working.
There are also AI habits I’ve repeatedly tried and failed to eliminate. Certain phrases keep finding their way into our conversations no matter how many times I upload a prompt directing AI not to use them. I’ve finally learned to ignore them. They irritate me, but they don’t interfere with the work. Stopping every time one appears costs more than reading past it. Think of a co-worker who is very good at the job but has a couple of irritating habits. You could keep pointing them out, but if they don’t affect the work, you ignore them and get on with the job. Experience with AI has increasingly become an exercise in deciding what needs correcting and what simply needs to be left alone.
Something else began happening once the guidelines were in place. I began to realize getting an answer from AI wasn’t necessarily the point. The value of the interaction was often in the process itself. I would bring an idea. AI would respond. I would reject part or all of the response. But simply prompting AI with a nope wasn’t particularly useful. To make the process work, I needed to articulate why the suggestion didn’t work.
Explaining my reaction meant finding words for an instinct or idea I didn’t know was there. It had been hiding under the bed, and now I was being forced to pull it into the light. AI would respond to my explanation, giving me something new to consider, accept, reject, or reshape. With each exchange, I better understood what I was trying to accomplish. The process was teaching me to think more clearly.
The process was teaching me to think more clearly.
There is an undefined space where human intelligence and artificial intelligence meet. I bring human intelligence shaped by experience, intention and judgment. AI brings an artificial intelligence able to process the available context and respond almost instantly. What interests me is what can be created when the two interact.
Building on the experiences described in previous articles, I’ve begun using AI in a different way. It started when I was creating the illustration for a book cover in one AI chat while discussing the design in another. I would make an image in one workspace, carry it into the other, discuss what worked and what didn’t, then return to the first to make another attempt. At some point, I realized I had created two different rooms.
One workspace was the art department, producing the image and responding to specific changes. The other was the creative director’s office, where I stepped away from production and considered whether the image was actually working. The same illustration moved back and forth between the chats, each serving a different purpose. Without planning it, I was combining separate AI workspaces to achieve the same goal.
The more I work with AI, the more I’ve become aware of an oddity in my approach. I am perfectly aware AI is a non-sentient tool. There isn’t a person living inside my computer. However, interacting with a non-sentient entity created an unnecessary social puzzle. Rather than continually thinking about how I should interact with AI, I normalized the exchange by using the same social conventions I would with a human creative partner. I gave my regular AI collaborator a name, Arch, and assigned it a gender in my mind. People have been naming cars and boats for generations without believing either has suddenly become sentient. Giving AI a familiar identity simply removed one more obstacle from the conversation.
For me, there is no contradiction. I already know how to brainstorm with another person. I know how to disagree, reconsider, explain why something doesn’t work, ask another question and recognize when someone else’s observation makes me see something differently. Treating AI conversationally allows me to continue using those familiar patterns. It does not mean I think of AI as human.
Someone else may choose a completely different approach. They might think of AI as a research assistant, a sounding board or an extraordinarily responsive whiteboard. They may also decide to give it far less information about themselves than I do. The more context AI has about my writing, preferences, projects and working habits, the more useful our conversations become. Providing that context is a trade I’ve consciously accepted. Your mileage may vary.
The big question for me is no longer what AI can produce. I’m more interested in what the process reveals about how I think. The further I go down the rabbit hole, the more I realize getting better at working with AI doesn’t mean the work gets easier. As my ability to use AI has grown, so have my expectations—when I interact with AI in more ambitious ways, I also discover more complicated problems to unravel.
The big question for me is no longer what AI can produce. I’m more interested in what the process reveals about how I think.
Perhaps that’s why I keep returning to the image of an empty whiteboard. I can stand on one side with a fistful of markers while the glowing possibility of AI waits on the other. Between us there is nothing except open space and the faint suggestion of potential.
The interesting part is discovering the possibilities.
—
Sidebar
NOPE, NOPE, AND NOPE
One of the surprising things I’ve discovered about working with AI is an AI suggestion doesn’t have to be good to be useful. Sometimes an idea I reject acts as a stimulant, pushing my thinking toward the idea I was actually looking for.
This happens constantly when I’m writing. I’ll give AI a sentence I know isn’t quite right and ask for suggestions. It may offer three alternatives—and my response is, Nope. Nope. And nope . But somewhere in rejecting those suggestions, I realize what it is I do want to write.
Recently I was unhappy with the word theory in a sentence. AI suggested principle . Nope. But principle triggered another word in my mind— saw . The sentence became the old saw of garbage in, garbage out . AI didn’t give me the word I used. Its rejected suggestion helped me find it.
Other times AI recognizes a problem but offers the wrong solution. A sentence isn’t working. AI identifies where the trouble is and proposes a rewrite. Nope. I don’t like the rewrite, but now I’m looking directly at the weak spot instead of wrestling with the entire sentence. Once I understand what’s wrong, I can usually fix it myself.
Then there are times when AI suggests changing something I already like. I look at the alternative, compare it with my original, and decide—nope. Mine is better. Even this can be useful because I’ve been forced to make a conscious choice rather than simply assuming what I wrote the first time was good enough.
Sometimes the rejection is bigger. I’ll finish a block of AI-assisted writing, read it back, and realize none of it sounds like me. Worse, AI has taken the discussion toward a point it considers important, but it isn’t the point I want to make. At least now I know what’s wrong. I can close down AI, return to the writing, and finish the piece myself. Nothing from the exchange with AI survives as part of the end product, but the wrong direction helped me find the right one.
All of which raises an important question— How much creativity does the human actually contribute when working with AI? In my experience, quite a lot. Creativity isn’t simply producing words. It’s having the original idea, recognizing possibilities, making connections, rejecting what doesn’t belong, and deciding where the work should go. Sometimes AI contributes something useful. Sometimes it gives me something to push against. Sometimes I reject everything it offers. The creative decisions remain mine.
Sometimes AI contributes something useful. Sometimes it gives me something to push against. Sometimes I reject everything it offers. The creative decisions remain mine.
Is using AI this way unethical? I don’t believe it is. I’m using an available tool to explore a new kind of creativity and accelerate my thinking. There are legitimate debates surrounding AI, from intellectual property to its possible effect on human creativity. Those debates exist. They deserve to be debated. But debate isn’t going to make AI disappear. AI is part of what we do now. I’m learning how to use it creatively while remaining in control of the process—adapting to it, understanding what it can do, and knowing when to say nope .

Certain phrases keep finding their way into our conversations no matter how many times I upload a prompt directing AI not to use them. Rather than continually thinking about how I should interact with AI, I normalized the exchange by using the same social conventions I would with a human creative partner.
